{"id": "19:79/q15", "question": "What occasion for the passage is reported?", "turns_on": "Whether the reported mocking debt episode fits the context's serious reasoning, and whether the claimant is identified as al-ʿĀṣ or al-Walīd.", "positions": [{"id": "19:79/q15/p1", "position": "Al-ʿĀṣ b. Wāʾil withheld a debt or wages from Khabbāb, demanded he disavow Muḥammad, then mockingly promised repayment from afterlife wealth and children.", "reasons": "Khabbāb's report is transmitted by Yaḥyā b. Sallām, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr and al-Bukhārī; al-Qurṭubī names Muslim and Bukhārī, while Ibn Kathīr notes several canonical routes. Al-Kalbī and Muqātil add that blacksmith Khabbāb made jewelry for al-ʿĀṣ, who mocked repayment in Paradise and claimed Khabbāb had no greater entitlement. These accounts vary between debt, wages and jewelry but describe the same withheld payment. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that a resurrection-denier's mockery does not fit the passage's serious reply."}, {"id": "19:79/q15/p2", "position": "The claimant may instead be al-Walīd b. al-Mughīra, named alongside al-ʿĀṣ in a majority explanation.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports the majority naming al-ʿĀṣ or al-Walīd and describing a claim of afterlife wealth and children, followed by God's questions about unseen knowledge or a covenant and by solitary return without possessions."}, {"id": "19:79/q15/p3", "position": "The statement should be understood as a serious claim, not a resurrection-denier's mockery.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that the reported mocking occasion is inconsistent with the passage answering by a serious argument."}]}
{"id": "19:79/q16", "question": "How does the preceding divine name al-Raḥmān sharpen the reply?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:79/q16/p1", "position": "It ironically evokes the mercy the unbeliever assumed would guarantee his prosperity and needles Quraysh for rejecting that name.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr links the irony to Quraysh's response to the name in 25:60."}]}
{"id": "19:80/q01", "question": "What does God inheriting what the man says mean?", "turns_on": "Whether mā denotes real possessions, imagined Paradise goods, the man's entire legacy, his recorded words, his continuing speech, or the man himself; the occasion report and the prior promise to record his words are invoked in the discussion.", "positions": [{"id": "19:80/q01/p1", "position": "God takes the man's actual worldly wealth and children at death, ending his ownership of them.", "reasons": "Mujāhid identifies al-ʿĀṣ's wealth and children (MUJAHID, YAḤYĀ, ṬABARĪ, IBN KATHĪR, DURR); Qatāda says all he possesses (YAḤYĀ, ʿABD AL-RAZZĀQ, ṬABARĪ, IBN KATHĪR, DURR). Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda and Ibn Zayd explain that destruction ends his ownership (WĀḤIDĪ, ṬABRISĪ, IBN AL-JAWZĪ); al-Zajjāj says it passes to others. Ibn Qutayba, Bayḍāwī, Bursawī and Ālūsī contrast real worldly goods with a baseless future boast; Ālūsī prefers this sense, reading mā as their substance. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls inheritance figurative dispossession, a threat of near death; his sons ʿAmr and Hishām became Muslims, bringing the Prophet good news and al-ʿĀṣ grief. Asad likewise calls it a metaphor for taking what had been vested in him. Al-Biqāʿī locates this at death; the Study Quran cites God as ultimate Inheritor (19:40, 15:23, 21:89, 28:58). Al-Kashshāf and Abū Ḥayyān mention the possibility that even hoped-for worldly goods, if granted, are later removed, comparing 6:94; Ālūsī finds that imagined grant very remote in light of the occasion report. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the failed hope an inherited disappointment."}, {"id": "19:80/q01/p2", "position": "God deprives him of the wealth and children he claimed for the Hereafter and assigns them to others.", "reasons": "Muqātil says the claimed reward goes to someone else; al-Farrāʾ chooses Paradise property for another. Al-Suddī and al-Kalbī specify gold, silver and silk for other Muslims (WĀḤIDĪ); Abū Suhayl says more deserving recipients (ABŪ ḤAYYĀN, ĀLŪSĪ). Ibn al-Jawzī reports Ibn ʿAbbās and says al-Farrāʾ selected it. Al-Kashshāf calls them the claimed goods given to someone deserving. Ālūsī says the interpretation presumes no procreation in Paradise. Wāḥidī adds that he also loses what he possessed here; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the hope disappointed. Māwardī presents this beside the worldly-wealth account."}, {"id": "19:80/q01/p3", "position": "God inherits everything the man amassed and did in worldly life.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd says nothing, small or great, accompanies him (ṬABARĪ and IBN KATHĪR); this extends the inherited object to his deeds as well as possessions."}, {"id": "19:80/q01/p4", "position": "God preserves the man's utterance as a charge to be used against him at judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī says it is retained for requital; al-Naḥḥās compares scholars inheriting prophets through preserving their words (IBN ʿAṬIYYA, ABŪ ḤAYYĀN). Al-Kashshāf says the record exposes and shames him at the gathering. Ālūsī observes that the earlier 'We shall write' already expresses preservation. Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads the man's surviving claim as a sin attached to him, with no worldly support left; he prefers this because the passage seriously rebuts the claim."}, {"id": "19:80/q01/p5", "position": "God ends the man's mocking speech when death overtakes him.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf says he speaks only while alive; Ālūsī says death reveals reality and ends further mockery. An objection that this assumes an unbeliever sincerely believed in resurrection is answered by saying mockery can continue until death."}, {"id": "19:80/q01/p6", "position": "God inherits the man himself.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās gives this concise gloss, without further explanation in the note."}]}
{"id": "19:80/q02", "question": "How is mā in 'We inherit him what he says' construed?", "turns_on": "The syntactic relation of mā to the object pronoun, and whether an omitted noun is needed because literal words cannot be inherited.", "positions": [{"id": "19:80/q02/p1", "position": "Mā is an appositive of inclusion or clarification to the object pronoun.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn calls it an appositive of inclusion. Bursawī cites al-ʿUyūn for an appositional reading that accompanies his destruction and transfer of wealth and children. Ālūsī says it explains the pronoun; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it an appositional clarification of the object pronoun, whose referent is actual property and children."}, {"id": "19:80/q02/p2", "position": "Mā is the direct object, with the attached pronoun implying 'from him'.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and Ālūsī present this syntactic alternative."}, {"id": "19:80/q02/p3", "position": "An omitted noun before mā means the sense or named referent of his words.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports this because words themselves cannot be inherited."}]}
{"id": "19:80/q03", "question": "What does 'what he says' refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the reported promise concerns goods in the next life or worldly goods, and whether the phrase includes the man's broader blasphemy and mockery.", "positions": [{"id": "19:80/q03/p1", "position": "His boast that he would receive wealth and children in the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Ṭabarī, al-Farrāʾ, al-Nasafī, the Study Quran and others identify the claim of future wealth and children; Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports the majority's reading as a sworn claim of Paradise goods after resurrection. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the short phrase compresses a lengthy boast and mockery and compares 3:183."}, {"id": "19:80/q03/p2", "position": "His claim to receive wealth and children in worldly life.", "reasons": "Bursawī says only the worldly goods actually given can be inherited, because the future boast has no object. Al-Kashshāf and Abū Ḥayyān entertain a hope for worldly wealth that could be granted and then removed; Ālūsī finds that suggestion remote given the occasion report. Ṭabāṭabāʾī's preferred account says he claimed disbelief would bring wealth and children and left that sinful claim behind."}, {"id": "19:80/q03/p3", "position": "His full blasphemy and mockery, compressed into a short phrase.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the concise reference to hostile words in 3:183. Al-Kashshāf and Ālūsī take the speech literally as continued mockery until death."}]}
{"id": "19:80/q04", "question": "Why does 'he says' use a present verb?", "turns_on": "Whether the present form recalls an earlier claim or depicts ongoing mockery until death.", "positions": [{"id": "19:80/q04/p1", "position": "Its sense recalls what the man already said.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān explicitly says the present form has past meaning. Ālūsī relates the tense to what the man had received; Ibn ʿĀshūr treats the expression as a compressed reference to his prior speech."}, {"id": "19:80/q04/p2", "position": "It portrays his repeated speech while he lives, which death will stop.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf and Ālūsī say the man keeps mocking while alive; death exposes reality and silences him."}]}

{"id": "19:80/q10", "question": "Does Paradise include procreation?", "turns_on": "The force and wording of the conditional Tirmidhī report, the reliability of the other report, and whether the no-child reports exclude all procreation or only ordinary reproduction.", "positions": [{"id": "19:80/q10/p1", "position": "Its people have no offspring there.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports Mujāhid, Ṭāwūs and Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī denying procreation, citing reports that Paradise's people have no offspring and a long report from Laqīṭ ibn ʿĀmir. {"id": "20:10/q25", "question": "What inward meaning is given to the fire and Moses' hopes?", "turns_on": "Different inward readings identify the fire with the Holy Spirit, divine manifestation, or spiritual awakening.", "positions": [{"id": "20:10/q25/p1", "position": "The fire is the Holy Spirit illuminating souls, and the family are Moses' faculties.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says the faculties remain still as sensory activity quiets; the firebrand is a luminous benefit to them, while finding a guide is gaining knowledge and gnosis leading to truth."}, {"id": "20:10/q25/p2", "position": "God appeared in the desired form of fire to draw Moses toward Him.", "reasons": "Bursevī transmits some Sufis' explanation that another form might have made Moses turn away; his poem says Moses did not yet recognize the divine manifestation in light and speech."}, {"id": "20:10/q25/p3", "position": "The fire symbolizes rising spiritual certainty.", "reasons": "The Study Quran adds the mountain of God, Horeb, from Exodus; Asad treats the lost road as a possible symbol of spiritual need and the fire as a burning-bush allegory.
